entries.name: Domestic dog
entries.spread: with people along every migration route from the Upper Palaeolithic; worldwide by the Neolithic
entries.notes: The oldest and most widespread domesticate; bred into hundreds of function-specific working types. Model as a companion and guard, not as prey or livestock.

entries.name: Domestic cat
entries.spread: Egypt and the Mediterranean with grain trade; worldwide with shipping from the Classical era on
needs: vermin-free shedding spaces are optional, they find their own
entries.notes: Half-tamed rather than bred: cats self-domesticated around grain stores and barely changed genetically. A cat is a working mouser that chose the humans.

entries.name: Chicken
entries.spread: South and Southeast Asia by 4000 BCE; Europe by the classical age; global after 1500 CE
entries.notes: The most numerous domesticated bird on Earth; initial spread likely driven by cockfighting and ritual more than meat. Keep flocks small in-game or they strip the grass bare.

entries.name: Taurine cattle
entries.spread: Europe, steppe and North Africa by 6000 BCE; the backbone of mixed farming everywhere it went
entries.notes: Milk, meat, hides, draught and dung in one animal; the whole farming year revolves around it. One aurochs herd per settlement is a reasonable baseline.

entries.name: Zebu (humped cattle)
entries.spread: Indian subcontinent, then East Africa and Southeast Asia; Brahman crosses worldwide today
entries.notes: The second, independent cattle domestication; better in hot dry scrub than taurine cattle. Distinguish by hump and dewlap when spawning hot-climate farms.

entries.name: Domestic pig

domesticated.where: Fertile Crescent (independently in China about 9000 years ago)

entries.spread: Europe and North Africa with Neolithic farmers; on ships and into the Americas after 1492
entries.notes: Fast to fat, eats nearly anything: the village larder. Note the two domestication lineages if you ever model ancestry; feral pigs reappear fast wherever fences drop.

entries.name: Domestic sheep
entries.spread: Mediterranean, steppe and eventually everywhere with farms; wool selected in Western Europe
entries.notes: Hair sheep first, woolly sheep after European selection; dual-purpose. A flock follows moving pasture, so in-game they pull against fixed-field agriculture.

entries.name: Domestic goat
entries.spread: Mediterranean, Arabia, then global; thrives where sheep fail
entries.notes: The poor family's cow: hardy, upright on rock, and notorious for stripping bark — they make overgrazed hillsides in fiction and in fact.

entries.name: Domestic horse
entries.spread: Steppe by 4000 BCE; chariot warfare carried it everywhere; universal farm and war animal by 1000 BCE
entries.notes: Botai horses may be ancestors of Przewalski's horse, with modern horses re-domesticated on the Pontic steppe; either way the domesticate is one species. In-game, horses change the map: day-rideable range and cavalry.

entries.name: Mallard duck
entries.spread: China and East Asia first; wherever paddy rice went, ducks went too
entries.notes: The rice farmer's partner: ducks weed and insect-proof paddies. Pekin-type breeds are heavy meat birds; egg production can outrun hens.

entries.name: Domestic goose
entries.wild_ancestor: greylag goose (Anser anser) and swan goose (Anser cygnoides)
entries.spread: Mediterranean and Europe (greylag), temperate China and East Asia (swan goose)
entries.notes: Two independent domesticities that cross-breed freely; European geese even predate Roman times. Geese are territorial noisemakers — good farmyard alarms.

entries.name: Domestic turkey
entries.spread: Mexico and the Southwest US; to Europe with the Spanish in the 1500s; global since
entries.notes: A New World domesticate that swapped hemispheres within a generation of 1492. Broad-breasted modern birds can barely breed naturally — a breeding fact worth stealing for design.

entries.name: Domestic donkey

domesticated.where: Egypt and the Horn of Africa

entries.spread: Along Nile and Red Sea trade routes; Mediterranean, Arabia and India; the poor person's horse everywhere
entries.notes: Tougher and thriftier than a horse, and smarter than its reputation; the desert and mountain pack animal. Sterile mules need both a donkey and a horse in the world model.

entries.name: Water buffalo

domesticated.where: Indian subcontinent (river type) and China (swamp type)

entries.spread: South and Southeast Asia with rice; to Italy and Egypt in antiquity; Brazil huge today
needs: draft work or none at all
entries.notes: Two domestications kept separate: river buffalo (India, dairy) vs swamp buffalo (China, draught). The muscle of the paddy; no buffalo, no easy rice terraces.

entries.name: Dromedary (one-humped camel)
entries.spread: Arabia and North Africa by 1500 BCE; Sahara trade and Islamic expansion carried it deep into Africa and Spain
entries.notes: Extinct in the wild; every dromedary alive is a feral or tame descendant of managed stock (Australia hosts a feral herd). The desert's ship: water-thrifty, caravan-defining.

entries.name: Bactrian camel (two-humped)
entries.spread: Silk Road oases: Persia, Central Asia, Mongolia, western China; never suited to the hot Sahara
needs: shade is optional, they like cold
entries.notes: The cold-desert counterpart to the dromedary; double-humped, shaggier, frost-hardy, and famously grumpy. Wild Bactrians still survive in China/Mongolia — critically endangered and never bred in captivity again.

entries.name: Domestic yak
entries.spread: Tibetan Plateau and Himalayas; Mongolia, Pamirs, Siberia fringes
needs: no lowland heat — they sicken and die
entries.notes: Oldest dated physical evidence is only ~2500 years BP, but language and genetics suggest earlier management on the plateau. The only true high-altitude pack-and-milk bovid; heat is lethal to them.

entries.name: Llama
entries.spread: Within the Andes by the pre-Inca era; global as a fancy and farm animal in the 20th century
entries.notes: The Andes' only pre-European beast of burden; Inca logistics ran on llama caravans. Spits when pushed; hard on soft feet, soft on hard loads; loads cap around 50 kg.

entries.name: Alpaca
entries.spread: Andean highlands; today farmed worldwide for fibre
entries.notes: Bred purely for fibre; wild cousins were reserved for Inca nobility. Finer and denser fleece than sheep at a fraction of the biomass — the luxury wool of the high puna.

entries.name: Domestic rabbit
entries.spread: Mediterranean with Romans (kept, not yet bred); southern French monasteries bred it by the 12th century; pets by the Victorian era
entries.notes: A slow domestication, Rome to about 1500; kittens in cages only worked out with selective breeding. Meat and fur in wars and farms; pet in cities; always chewing cable insulation.

entries.name: Guinea pig (cuy)
entries.spread: Indigenous Andean cookery for millennia; Europe from the 1500s as an exotic pet
entries.notes: Raised for meat (cuy) in the high Andes to this day; arrived at European courts as a cavy pet. Colony-breeding, extreme reproduction rate, absurdly vocal for its size.

entries.name: Domestic pigeon
entries.spread: With every city after Mesopotamia; message-carrying until the telegraph; squab farming worldwide
entries.notes: Possibly domesticated earlier still (claims reach 10,000 years); cuneiform tablets from over 5000 years ago mention it. Homing ability is why empires could talk to themselves — and why cities are now full of feral rock doves.

entries.name: Japanese quail
entries.spread: Japan first, then Korea and China; laboratory staple worldwide since the 20th century
entries.notes: Raised first for song contests, then eggs (a hen lays nearly an egg a day) and later as a lab animal. Pocket-sized poultry: an egg ration for a cramped hermit or a spaceship.

entries.name: Ferret
entries.spread: Romans spread it through Europe for rabbiting; to England before the Norman conquest
entries.notes: The ferret is a tool, not a pet: put it down a rabbit hole and the rabbit comes out. Long, limbless-feeling body built for burrows; mustelid mischief in a tube.

entries.name: Reindeer

domesticated.where: Arctic Siberia and Scandinavia (independently, at least twice)

entries.spread: Circumpolar north: Sápmi (Scandinavia), Nenetsia, Siberia, Mongolia, Alaska (introduced) and Canada
entries.notes: Semi-domesticated, still perfectly capable of going feral and interbreeding with caribou; herding is more like delayed capture than breeding. The only large-scale domesticated deer, and the engine of Arctic pastoralism.

entries.name: Helmeted guinea fowl

domesticated.where: sub-Saharan Africa (domestic form recorded in Greece by the 5th century BCE)

entries.spread: Africa to the classical Mediterranean; now French cuisine, tick control in the Americas and feral everywhere
entries.notes: Domestication timing genuinely unknown; Africa origin, Greece by 5th century BCE. Loud, social, tick-eating alarm systems that lay dark speckled eggs.

entries.name: Mithun (gayal)
entries.spread: Northeast India, Bhutan, Bangladesh hill tracts and northern Burma / Yunnan fringes
entries.notes: Semi-domesticated at best; kept as wealth and prestige, not for milk or meat. Rare bovid you meet only in the eastern Himalaya — a status animal, not a working one.

entries.name: Asian working elephant
entries.wild_ancestor: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) — never genetically domesticated
entries.spread: South and Southeast Asia: logging, war, temples and ceremony
entries.notes: Not truly domesticated: stock is captured from the wild in each generation and tamed, never bred for tameness. Mohenjo-daro seals show tamed elephants; they powered logging into the 20th century. In-game: siege/haulage, huge upkeep.

entries.name: Muscovy duck
entries.spread: Aztec and other Amerindian cultures; carried to Europe on Columbus's Santa Maria (1500s); now feral worldwide
entries.notes: The only domesticated duck neither from the mallard line nor from Eurasia; hisses, walks, roosts in rafters. Amerindians bred it for meat before 1492; timing unrecorded.

entries.name: Common carp
entries.spread: China >5000 BCE; Romans farmed it on the Danube; European monks spread it 13th–16th century; now global and invasive
entries.notes: The world's first farmed fish, and famously indestructible — feed the family Friday fish from holes in the ground. Koi is its ornamental offshoot; escaped carp now wreck freshwater ecosystems worldwide.

entries.name: Goldfish
entries.spread: Jin-dynasty China records orange mutations; Song dynasty (1162) imperial pond; Japan and Europe by 1500s
entries.notes: First orange individuals noted in the Jin dynasty, but sustained selective breeding is a Song-dynasty invention reserved for emperors. The cheapest, most forgiving ornamental animal ever bred.

entries.name: Nile tilapia
entries.spread: Farmed in Egypt >4000 years ago (tomb art shows ponds); selectively bred only in the 20th century; farmed worldwide today
entries.notes: Shown in man-made ponds in Egyptian tomb paintings, so kept rather than ever bred truly tame; modern 'improved' strains are recent. Mouthbroods its young — a rare breeding style among food fish.

entries.name: Betta (Siamese fighting fish)
entries.spread: Thai villages and courts; exported to the West in the 1800s as a fighting and ornamental fish
needs: one male per water space (they fight)
entries.notes: Bred for aggression first, beauty second — the original gambling fish. Huge finned forms postdate the export; wild ancestors are drably short-finned. Great colour payoff per litre of tank.

entries.name: Silkworm (domesticated silk moth)
entries.spread: Yangshao culture China; smuggled to Korea, Japan, Byzantium and Venice by the early Middle Ages
entries.notes: Cannot survive in the wild any more: wingless, blind, flock-reared — pure caterpillar monoculture for silk. Beyond honey one of the few farmed insects; also silk's foundation in every economy from Hangzhou to Genoa.

entries.name: Western honey bee
entries.wild_ancestor: wild western honey bee (Apis mellifera) — never truly domesticated
entries.spread: Egyptian and Near Eastern apiaries; through Europe with monastic beekeeping; Americas after 1600
needs: foraging range of flowers/ trees within ~3 km
entries.notes: Managed for at least 4400 years (apiaries in the sun temple of Ne-user-re, ~2400 BCE), but any colony can walk out and live wild. Honey, wax, pollination — the only farm animal that also farms its surroundings.

entries.name: Cochineal insect
entries.wild_ancestor: cactus scale insects in the Dactylopius genus (native Mexican species)
entries.spread: Aztec tribute lists pre-1519; Spanish monopoly exports founded the dye trade from Oaxaca to Europe for 200 years
needs: drying and brushing for dye cakes
entries.notes: Not bred but reared on cactus pads: a dye farm, not an animal farm. Carminic acid gives scarlet and crimson — the red of Renaissance cardinals, British redcoats and, today, food colouring E120.
